s04.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 7 · 3:25 PM · DELGADO HALL, 420 — SUPER BOWL XLIV

journal.title: Doug Pruitt
journal.text: Doug Pruitt. 420, with Kevin. Bakersfield. Mechanical engineering. A Tauren druid. Says ‘dude’ with five vowels. Tuesday the 8th, 3:58 in the morning, I caught his wrist on the east-stair pull station. He was asleep. The raid boss was in the elevator. Super Bowl Sunday on his futon with Yusuf, the surround sound wired for the island and now for this. He stood up on the futon for the onside kick. When Theo called from the street he screamed *who dat* into my phone and New Orleans screamed it back. He cried at the bell in *It’s a Wonderful Life*.

body: At 3:02 the sun comes through the window of 420 at the one angle that defeats a television, and Doug has beaten it with a bedsheet, a roll of duct tape and four hours of conviction.

The Logitech is up. Five speakers on a long sagging loop of wire are duct-taped along the bookshelf on Kevin’s half of the room, which is otherwise untouched: the bed made tight enough to bounce a quarter, the label maker, an orgo flowchart in a plastic sleeve. On Kevin’s pillow there’s an index card he left Friday morning, *DISCLOSURE: I HAVE NOT AUTHORIZED THIS*, and under it, in Doug’s marker, *dude it sounds amazing*.

Doug is in a black Brees jersey with the Big 5 fold lines still across the chest. “For solidarity,” he says, when Jack looks. “With who?” “Dude. Everybody.” He taps the chip in the doorjamb as Jack comes in under it, the quarter-sized wound from the futon run. “History.”

The futon sags in the middle like a hammock somebody gave up on. The frame came out of the fourth-floor lounge and the mattress out of a donation bin, and Jack carried the heavy end, which in moral theology makes him a cooperator in evil, remote and material. Yusuf is on the floor with his back against it and a legal pad on his knee, on which he has drawn the field and cut it into zones he declines to explain. On an upturned laundry basket sit three bags of chips and, apart from them, a fourth, sealed, with a Post-it in Kevin’s hand: *THESE ARE THE HEALTHY ONES. — K.T.*
“Not the healthy ones,” Doug says, indicating the three, gravely. “I want to be really clear.”
The RAZR goes off against Jack’s hip as he sits.

body.text: POP IS FOR THE SAINTS BC THEY SUFFERED

body: That is Frank’s entire philosophy of sport, and it has been right about Cleveland every year since 1964.
“Who are we against?” Doug says.
“The Colts.” Jack takes a handful of the unhealthy ones. “They left Baltimore in the middle of the night in Mayflower vans. In Ohio we know what it means when the vans come at night.”
“Duuude,” says Doug, with feeling, and settles in to hate Indianapolis.

By the end of the first quarter the Colts are up 10–0, and Doug has said *It’s fine* so many times that it has stopped being a sentence. “It’s *fine*,” he tells the screen. “It’s a first-pull wipe. You don’t disband the raid.” He looks over at Jack for the first time since the coin toss. “Dude, you look like you slept in a bus station.”
“I’m good.”
“Cool.” Yusuf glances up from the pad and back down, and draws a line.

body.text: Celeste has asked me to stop standing. I can’t. I’m Catholic.

body: “Kevin’s standing,” Jack says. “Kevin stands for everything,” says Doug. “He stood for the Pledge in the *car*.”

At the half it’s Colts 10, Saints 6, and the Who come out in a blaze of white light, and the synthesizer that opens *Baba O’Riley* starts up out of five duct-taped speakers and fills 420 to the corners.
“Dude, these guys are like *sixty*.”
“That’s the point of them,” says Yusuf.

body.text: motel tv has rabbit ears. the who is OLD. is this what u people like
tell frank i watched it on rabbit ears for him. we are the same now

body: “Is that Skye?” Doug asks. “She says the Who are old.” Doug is hurt in some deep place, and turns the surround up.

The second half opens with the Saints lining up to kick off, and something is wrong with the formation, and Doug says “They’re not—” and they are. The ball squibs ten yards and disappears under a pile of men in black and gold and white, and the referee digs through it, and comes up pointing the Saints’ way. Doug is on the futon, on his feet, and the frame makes a sound like a car accident and holds.
“That is insane,” says Yusuf, who has put down the pen, with something near reverence. “They removed the factor of safety. On purpose. At kickoff.”
Jack is up too, both hands on top of his head, standing on Doug’s rug in his socks and yelling at the Super Bowl.

With three minutes left, and 420 gone quiet enough to hear the subwoofer breathing, Peyton Manning throws for the sideline and Tracy Porter is simply there, as if he’d been issued the ball, and takes it all the way back with the fourth floor behind him.
“Load-bearing interception,” Yusuf says, not looking up from the pad.
Doug is no longer on the futon. He’s on the rug, face down, screaming into it. Saints 31, Colts 17, and the last minutes are a formality that the three of them watch to the end anyway.

body.text: Finding: grown men are weeping in a kitchen. I am not permitted to take notes.

body: Yusuf tears the top sheet off the legal pad, folds it in four, and puts it in his shirt pocket. “For the record,” he says, “the zones were wrong.” Doug leans down over the back of the futon and hugs him around the neck, and Yusuf allows it for the length of one breath.

The RAZR rings at 7:09, THEO VANCE (IMPORTANT) across the little screen, and Jack opens it a foot from his ear and the city comes out. Horns, hundreds of them, no two on the same note. A brass band somewhere off the phone’s left shoulder, tuba first, moving. A stranger leans into Theo’s phone and screams *WHO DAT*, and Doug, who has crossed the room without being asked, screams it back into the RAZR from six inches, and the stranger screams it back again, hoarse and joyful, at a boy in a dormitory he will never meet.
“Costigan.” Theo, over all of it. “Are you hearing this? This is a city that has been told no for forty-three years.” Forty-three years is three more than the Israelites got, and they had a cloud.

response: Theo says nothing, and into the gap goes the brass band, tuba first.
“So am I,” he says. No pitch in it anywhere, none of the cashmere. “Mostly.”

response.text: “And I’m not spending my *anything* on a football game, Costigan. I’m saving it.” The line fills up with tuba and goes dead.
response.else: He hangs up into the brass band.

response: “You don’t get to say that, Costigan. You’re from *Ohio*. You people say *O-H*.”
“He has a point,” Yusuf says, from the floor.

response.text: “And I’m not spending my *anything* on a football game, Costigan. I’m saving it.” The line fills up with tuba and goes dead.
response.else: He hangs up into the brass band.

choices.text: *Hold the phone up and let Doug have it.*
response: Doug takes the RAZR in both hands, like a chalice, carries it to the middle of the rug, and screams into it with everything he has left. New Orleans screams back. He screams again.
“That’s a call and response,” says Yusuf. “It’s liturgical.”
Jack gets the phone back in time for the end of it.

response.text: “And I’m not spending my *anything* on a football game, Costigan. I’m saving it.” The line fills up with tuba and goes dead.

s06.slug: MONDAY, FEBRUARY 8 – TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 9 · DELGADO → DEL PLAYA → THE ANCHOR
body: Monday, Priya does her rounds with a clipboard and stops in the open door of 412, where Theo’s bed is made with hospital corners and nobody is in it. “Per the Residential Life Handbook,” she says, “an absent roommate is still a roommate. I’m going to need you to water his plant.” “He doesn’t have a plant.” “Then I’m going to need you to not let him get one.” Doug, per Yusuf, wore the jersey to a lecture on stress and strain and was asked by the professor to sit down.
Monday night he takes the next case down off Theo’s stack, and the Post-it is on the lid in fountain pen, the capitals leaning into a wind.

SAT’s *Rififi* is still at the bottom of the stack in its case, uncracked. He’s a film behind and he is staying there. He watches the trenches of *Paths of Glory* on the MacBook with the lights off, and at the end a German girl, scared stiff on a tavern stage, starts to sing to a room of French soldiers who came in to jeer her, and the room goes quiet, and some of them begin to hum.

body.text: Finding #3: the matriarchy is real. I have been fed eleven times. I have not been asked one question I could answer with a citation.

body: He never received Finding #2. He has decided it was classified.
Tuesday at 1:16, in the Commons line with a tray and nothing on it yet, Theo:

body.text: The parade. One trophy, a great many people, and a policeman crying into a beignet. Celeste wept on a stranger. The stranger wept back. I have never been so moved by a piece of hardware.

body: A picture message follows. The RAZR thinks about it all the way down the salad bar and hands him a stamp: a bar in lamplight, a squat glass, something amber, a twist of peel on the rim. No caption. Theo has never in his life sent a picture without a caption; he captions weather. Jack reads the text twice and the stamp once and answers neither.

Afternoon, and he starts the Saab at the curb on Del Playa, because he was told twice a week and it has been three days. It stalls pulling out. It stalls again at the foot of Sol’s steps, and on the porch Tomás, wet-haired, in from the water, with a mug, has gone still in his chair to watch like a man at a ballgame. The third time it catches, runs rough for a block, and then doesn’t.
Tomás lifts the mug as Jack rolls past. “She was sulking.”
“I was warned.”
He sits a minute at the foot of the steps with the engine running. In the second-floor window of Sol’s house the curtain is still half open, the way she left it.

Idling at the corner with the engine finally behaving, he gets Ohio, at 3:40. The RAZR builds the picture slowly, in strips, and at the end of it there’s a white hump at a curb that has to be the Silverado, and a driveway, and in the driveway, small, in his black church coat, behind the snowblower like a plow horse with a grudge, Frank.

pop says the rodent was right and hes furious

body: For the first time since January there is nothing from Laney. No gag, no photo, no *fireman*. The inbox goes Gina, Gina, Theo, Margot, Skye, Skye, and then it goes back to last week.

Tuesday night the Anchor has three customers and a ballgame on Rudy’s transistor, which makes it a crowd. The board by the register says PIE OF THE DAY: OLALLIEBERRY. Merle, at the counter in his bibs with his decaf, has been unbearable about the Saints since Sunday; he put twenty on them at the Tackle Box and wants it understood that he never once doubted.
Gloria sets a bus tub on the table by the Hobart hard enough to settle the silverware.
“Every night.”
“Good.” She slides the top plate off the stack and puts it in his hands. “Now wash your hands, hon. You’re smiling at a pie tin.”
Rudy, at the grill, without looking up from *Flint*: “Mijo. The tin.”
The RAZR goes off in his apron pocket at 9:58, against the wet. He dries a thumb on his shirt and opens it.

body.text: You asked me what I wanted instead. I still don’t have an answer. I have a Valentine’s question.
Clare is in Marisol. I’m in New Orleans East with forty relatives and a florist’s website. Valentine’s is Sunday. I have a budget and no data.

choices.key: You told Kevin to send Clare red flowers and sign the card himself.

response.text: The website wants to know what the card should say. I’ve typed “Kevin” four times and deleted it three.

choices.text: “rosin. a violinist cant play a rose.”
choices.key: You told Kevin to send Clare rosin, because a violinist can’t play a rose.

response.text: Her violin is from 1911. I am going to research gauge until I die.

choices.key: You told Kevin to write Clare a letter in his own handwriting.

response.text: My handwriting is a medical liability.

choices.key: You told Kevin to ask Clare’s brothers.
response: An hour later, at the Hobart, with the last of the tins:

response.text: They voted. 3–1 for a Sharks jersey. The dissent was chocolate. I’m sending both. That’s democracy.
